text.p: Blue-chip stocks staged a late recovery from deep losses Wednesday as bargain-hunters and strength in Philip Morris came to the market's rescue.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended down 19.75 points at 6,422.94 after shaking off a loss of more than 75 points.
The rebound came one day after the index of 30 blue-chip stocks dropped 79 points due to heavy profit-taking.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances 1,426 to 1,041 on active volume of 493 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Nasdaq Composite index, however, snapped its seven straight sessions of record closes, ending off 3.35 points at 1,297.02.
Analysts were impressed with the Dow's rebound.
"The sell-off is over," said James Cramer, president of Cramer Co. "We had an unbelievable comeback and buyers came out of the woodwork..."

The Dow's recovery was helped by Philip Morris Cos. Inc, which gained 2 to 105-1/4 after Oppenheimer & Co. reiterated a buy rating on the stock. Another Dow component, J.P. Morgan rose 2-1/4 to 93-5/8.
Smaller-name stocks continued to outperform larger companies.

"It's part of the move from big cap names which have had such a dramatic move," said Jim Pizzo, senior investment strategist at Oppenheimer. "People are positioning themselves into smaller cap names, and we could get decent action going into them through January and February."

Weighing on stocks during the afternoon was news that Salomon Bros. cut the stock holdings in its recommended portfolio to 45 percent from 50 percent, moving the 5 percent to cash. The allocation is now 20 percent cash, 35 percent bonds and 45 percent stocks.
Salomon's Chief Equity Strategist David Shulman said that based on a "price/sales basis, valuations are the highest in history."
"I see at best a sideways market next year or at worst down 10-15 percent. A correction, not a bear market," he said. "We had two wonderful years so we may have a pause."
Drug, interest-rate sensitive stocks and some technology issues came under profit-taking pressure.

International Business Machines was off 1-3/8 to 161-3/4, Cisco Systems lost 2-1/4 to 63-1/4, Pfizer sank 1-1/2 to 83-7/8, and Merck & Co. was off 1/4 to 80-3/4. Wells Fargo lost 4-1/4 to 275-1/4 and Freddie Mac was off 3-1/2 to 108-1/8.
Continental Airlines Class B shares rose 2-3/8 to 30-3/4 and Delta Air Lines was up 1/2 at 75-1/4. Both airlines declined comment on reports that they are in merger talks.
GT Interactive slumped 4-3/4 to 7-7/8 after warning that its fourth-quarter income and revenues will fall short of Wall Street expectations.
U.S. Robotics rose 3-1/8 to 76-7/8 after Hitachi PC Corp. said it would use the modem maker's high-speed "x2" technology in its notebook computers.

Flextronics slumped 9 to 28-1/4. The company said it expects to take charges and restructuring costs of $5 million to $7 million and will be "modestly profitable" in the third and fourth quarters of fiscal 1997.
Restaurant operator CKE Restaurants added 2-5/8 to 34-1/2 on strong earnings for the latest quarter.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks fell 3.18 points to 745.10. The American Stock Exchange index was off 3.19 to 588.99.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 1.62 to 393.23. The average share was down 17 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,219.720 down 30.736 or 0.42 percent.
